questions.stem: Which of the following statements about microeconomics and macroeconomics <u>is not</u> true?

options.A: The study of very large industries is a topic within macroeconomics.
options.B: Macroeconomics is concerned with economy-wide phenomena.
options.C: Microeconomics is concerned with the specification of prices of individual goods.
options.D: Microeconomics and macroeconomics cannot be entirely separated.

explanation_steps: Microeconomics studies individual units – households, firms, particular markets and INDUSTRIES (however large). Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole (national income, inflation, unemployment).
B, C and D are true (macro builds on micro decisions, so the two cannot be fully separated). A is false: an industry, even a very large one, is a micro topic. Answer: A.
tips: Micro = parts (a firm, an industry, the price of one good); macro = the whole economy (GDP, general price level, total employment).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements <u>is true</u> about the impact of an increase in the price of cappuccino if cappuccino and cakes are complementary goods?

options.A: The demand for cappuccino will decrease.
options.B: The supply of cappuccino will decrease.
options.C: The equilibrium price and quantity of cakes will rise.
options.D: The equilibrium price and quantity of cakes will fall.

explanation_steps: A rise in the price of cappuccino reduces the QUANTITY demanded of cappuccino (a movement along its demand curve) – not its demand. So A is false, and E (A and D) is false too.
Cakes are consumed together with cappuccino, so fewer cappuccinos → the DEMAND for cakes decreases (shifts left).
With an unchanged supply of cakes, a leftward shift in demand lowers both the equilibrium price and quantity of cakes. Answer: D.
tips: Own price change → change in quantity demanded; price of a complement → shift in demand.
Trap: E looks attractive but A confuses ‘demand’ with ‘quantity demanded’.

questions.stem: One of the following <u>will not</u> shift the supply of cars to the right.

options.A: an increase in the price of cars.
options.B: an advance in the technology used to manufacture cars.
options.C: a decrease in the wage of workers employed to manufacture cars.
options.D: consumers’ expectations of lower fuel prices in the future.

explanation_steps: B (better technology) and C (lower wages = lower input costs) increase supply – the curve shifts right.
A: a change in the good's OWN price causes a movement along the supply curve (change in quantity supplied), not a shift.
D: consumers' expectations affect DEMAND for cars, not supply – so D does not shift supply either.
Keyed A (the textbook contrast between quantity supplied and supply); D also accepted.
tips: Own price → movement along the curve. Consumers' income, tastes and expectations → demand, not supply.

questions.stem:
Suppose we have the following market supply and demand schedules for Mobile Phone: (4 points)
Price (US $) | Quantity demanded | Quantity supplied: 300 | 7000 | 3000;  400 | 6000 | 4000;  500 | 5000 | 5000;  600 | 4000 | 6000;  700 | 3000 | 7000;  800 | 2000 | 8000.
2.1 What is the equilibrium price of mobile phones?
2.2 What is the equilibrium quantity of mobile phones?
2.3 If the price of mobile phones were $300 how much is the shortage?
2.4 If the price of mobile phones were $700 how much is the surplus?
explanation_steps: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded = quantity supplied: at $500 both are 5,000.
At $300 (below equilibrium): Qd 7,000 > Qs 3,000 → shortage (excess demand) of 4,000.
At $700 (above equilibrium): Qs 7,000 > Qd 3,000 → surplus (excess supply) of 4,000.
tips: Below equilibrium → shortage; above → surplus.
Give quantities with units (phones).

explanation_steps: Ped = −66.7% ÷ 66.7% = −1 → unit elastic.

questions.stem:
It is December 31 and time for your business to close the books. The following balances appear on the books of Didi Enterprises:
a. Didi, Drawing, $2,800.
b. Service revenue, $15,300.
c. Expense account balances: Salary, $9,000; Rent, $5,000; Advertising, $3,500.
Instruction:
4.1 Journalize the closing entries for Didi Enterprises. (4 points)
4.2 Compute the ending balance of Didi, capital by assuming the beginning balance of Didi, Capital is $25,000. (1 point)
questions.answer:
4.1 Dec 31: (1) Dr Service Revenue 15,300 / Cr Income Summary 15,300. (2) Dr Income Summary 17,500 / Cr Salary Expense 9,000, Cr Rent Expense 5,000, Cr Advertising Expense 3,500. (3) Net loss 2,200: Dr Didi, Capital 2,200 / Cr Income Summary 2,200. (4) Dr Didi, Capital 2,800 / Cr Didi, Drawing 2,800.
4.2 Ending capital = 25,000 − 2,200 − 2,800 = $20,000.

4.1 Closing entries – Didi Enterprises (general journal)
Date    | Account titles and explanation                       | P/R |   Debit |  Credit
--------+------------------------------------------------------+-----+---------+--------
Dec. 31 | Service Revenue                                      |     | $15,300 |
        | Income Summary                                       |     |         | $15,300
        | (To close the revenue account)                       |     |         |
31      | Income Summary                                       |     | $17,500 |
        | Salary Expense                                       |     |         |  $9,000
        | Rent Expense                                         |     |         |  $5,000
        | Advertising Expense                                  |     |         |  $3,500
        | (To close the expense accounts)                      |     |         |
31      | Didi, Capital                                        |     |  $2,200 |
        | Income Summary                                       |     |         |  $2,200
        | (To close Income Summary – net loss 17,500 − 15,300) |     |         |
31      | Didi, Capital                                        |     |  $2,800 |
        | Didi, Drawing                                        |     |         |  $2,800
        | (To close the drawing account)                       |     |         |

4.2 Didi, Capital – ending balance
                                 |       $
---------------------------------+--------
Didi, Capital, beginning         |  25,000
Less: Net loss (15,300 − 17,500) | (2,200)
Less: Withdrawals (drawing)      | (2,800)
Didi, Capital, ending            |  20,000

subparts.question: Journalize the closing entries
subparts.answer: Revenue → Income Summary 15,300; Income Summary 17,500 → expenses; Capital 2,200 → Income Summary (net loss); Capital 2,800 → Drawing.

explanation_steps: Total expenses = 9,000 + 5,000 + 3,500 = 17,500 > revenue 15,300 → NET LOSS of 2,200.
Close revenue to Income Summary (credit balance 15,300), then expenses (debit 17,500) → Income Summary has a 2,200 debit balance.
A debit balance (loss) is closed by debiting Capital and crediting Income Summary.
Drawing is closed directly to Capital.
Ending capital = 25,000 − 2,200 (loss) − 2,800 (drawing) = 20,000.
marking_points: 1 point each for the four closing entries (revenue, expenses, net loss to capital, drawing).
Closing expenses before revenue is equally acceptable.
tips: Check the sign of the result first: if expenses exceed revenue, the Income Summary entry is reversed.
Drawing never goes through Income Summary.

questions.stem:
Prepare the journal entries to record the following transactions on Albert Company’s general journal using periodic inventory system. (2.5 points)
a. On March 12, Dong Company sold $400,000 of merchandise to Albert Company, terms 2/10, n/30.
b. On March 16, Albert Company returned $50,000 of the merchandise purchased on March 12.
c. On March 21, Albert Company paid the balance due to Dong Company.
questions.answer:
Mar 12: Dr Purchases 400,000 / Cr Accounts Payable 400,000. Mar 16: Dr Accounts Payable 50,000 / Cr Purchase Returns and Allowances 50,000. Mar 21: Dr Accounts Payable 350,000 / Cr Purchase Discounts 7,000 / Cr Cash 343,000.

Albert Company – General Journal (periodic inventory system)
Date    | Account titles and explanation                                      | P/R |    Debit |   Credit
--------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+-----+----------+---------
Mar. 12 | Purchases                                                           |     | $400,000 |
        | Accounts Payable – Dong Company                                     |     |          | $400,000
        | (Purchased merchandise on account, terms 2/10, n/30)                |     |          |
16      | Accounts Payable – Dong Company                                     |     |  $50,000 |
        | Purchase Returns and Allowances                                     |     |          |  $50,000
        | (Returned merchandise to Dong Company)                              |     |          |
21      | Accounts Payable – Dong Company                                     |     | $350,000 |
        | Purchase Discounts                                                  |     |          |   $7,000
        | Cash                                                                |     |          | $343,000
        | (Paid the balance within the discount period: 2% × 350,000 = 7,000) |     |          |

subparts.label: b
subparts.question: March 16 return
subparts.answer: Dr Accounts Payable 50,000 / Cr Purchase Returns and Allowances 50,000

subparts.label: c
subparts.question: March 21 payment
subparts.answer: Dr Accounts Payable 350,000 / Cr Purchase Discounts 7,000 / Cr Cash 343,000

answer_tables.title: Albert Company – General Journal (periodic inventory system)
rows: (Paid the balance within the discount period: 2% × 350,000 = 7,000)

explanation_steps: This is the BUYER's (Albert's) journal. Under the periodic system merchandise bought is debited to Purchases (not Merchandise Inventory).
Returns reduce what is owed: Dr Accounts Payable, Cr Purchase Returns and Allowances 50,000.
Balance owed = 400,000 − 50,000 = 350,000. March 21 is within 10 days of March 12 (discount period ends March 22), so the 2% discount applies.
marking_points: 0.5 point each: March 12 and March 16 entries.
1.5 points: March 21 – Accounts Payable 350,000 (0.5), Purchase Discounts 7,000 (0.5), Cash 343,000 (0.5).
tips: The discount is on the amount owed AFTER returns.
Periodic: Purchases, Purchase Returns and Allowances, Purchase Discounts. Perpetual would credit Merchandise Inventory instead.
